context_quotes:
Follow the repository's existing conventions and `.editorconfig`. Prefer modern
C# features when they improve clarity, but do not rewrite working code solely
to use newer syntax. Consistency and readability matter more than maximizing
use of language features.

Primary constructors are appropriate when dependency injection or simple
initialization remains clear:

Use a regular constructor when validation or initialization is non-trivial,
explicit fields improve readability, the existing codebase consistently uses
that style, or parameter capture would make the class harder to understand. Do
not convert constructors mechanically.

## Records and Classes

Use records when value semantics and immutability are desirable, for example
many DTOs and genuine Value Objects. Use classes when identity, mutable
lifecycle, inheritance, or framework behavior makes class semantics clearer. Do
not turn every DTO or Domain type into a record automatically.

## Visibility and Inheritance

Keep implementation details non-public when they are not part of the project's
public API. Use `sealed` when a type is deliberately not intended for
inheritance and the modifier communicates useful design intent; do not add
`sealed` merely as a speculative JIT optimization.

## Modern Syntax and Type Inference

Use collection expressions, pattern matching, switch expressions,
target-typed construction, and other modern features when they make the code
easier to read; do not prefer newer syntax when the result is less obvious. Use
`var` when the type is obvious from the right-hand side or not important to
understanding the code; use an explicit type when it improves clarity.

## Naming

Use standard .NET naming: PascalCase for types, methods, properties, and public
members; camelCase for parameters and local variables; meaningful names over
abbreviations. Private-field naming follows the repository's established
convention.

Register validators with `FluentValidation.DependencyInjectionExtensions` and
follow the project's established validation invocation pattern rather than
adding a second competing mechanism.

Use stable constants for policy names repeated across the application.

## Roles

Roles fit when the business authorization model is genuinely role-oriented.
Avoid scattering compound role strings; prefer a policy when several roles or
claims represent one capability.

TypeScript, or lint failures merely to make verification pass.
- Preserve architecture and project conventions while fixing.
- Stop when progress has clearly stalled rather than making speculative edits.

Follow an existing branch-naming convention when one exists. Otherwise clear
prefixes such as `feature/`, `fix/`, `refactor/`, `test/`, `docs/`, and
`chore/` are reasonable defaults. Use meaningful names, and do not rename an
existing user branch merely to satisfy this convention.

Use modern language features when they make code clearer, safer, or simpler;
do not modernize code merely to demonstrate newer syntax.

Prefer a normal constructor when initialization, validation, field naming, or
debugging is clearer that way.

Use them when the target type is clear:

Do not replace every existing collection initializer solely for modernization.

Good candidates: immutable transport DTOs, genuine Value Objects, immutable
messages. Entities with identity and lifecycle remain classes unless the model
genuinely benefits from record semantics.

Use `required` when initializing a property is part of the type's valid
construction contract:

Do not use `required` as a substitute for constructor or domain validation where
invariants must be protected.

Avoid deeply nested patterns that are harder to read than straightforward

Use it to remove an otherwise trivial backing field; do not rewrite manual

Prefer immutability when it represents the model naturally; do not force it onto
framework models or workflows where controlled mutation is simpler.

Confirm that the project's configured language version supports a feature
before using it. Changing `LangVersion` or the target framework is a stack
decision, not a modernization step.

When explicitly asked to modernize code: preserve behavior, keep the change
focused, prefer readability improvements, build and test afterward, and do not
mix unrelated architecture refactoring into syntax modernization.

Newest syntax for its own sake; converting every class to a record;
`record struct` merely to avoid allocations; `Span<T>` without a performance
reason; deeply nested patterns; mass constructor conversion.

Do not force an established project to match this template when doing so
provides no concrete value.

Within a feature or service area, make each supporting type's responsibility
clear from its name, its immediate directory, or both. Prefer established
suffixes: `Service` (use-case orchestration), `Dto` (data transfer),
`Request`/`Response` (Application operation contracts; HTTP transport contracts
belong to Api), `Result`/`Outcome` (operation results), `Validator`,
`Rules`/`Policy` (decision or workflow rules), `Factory`, `Mapper`, `Adapter`.

Avoid ambiguous names such as `TaskWorkflow` when the role cannot be inferred
without opening the file; prefer `TaskWorkflowRules`, `TaskWorkflowPolicy`, or
`TaskWorkflowService` according to the actual responsibility. Add
responsibility-specific subdirectories only when a flat directory becomes hard
to navigate, and avoid generic `Models`, `Helpers`, `Common`, or `Utils`
buckets when a more specific responsibility can be named.

Keep deterministic repository-wide formatting and code-style configuration in
`.editorconfig`; prefer enforceable tooling configuration over restating
mechanical formatting rules in instructions.

# Repository-wide formatting and code-style configuration.
# Deterministic formatting belongs here rather than in Claude instructions
# (.claude/rules/coding-style.md defers to this file).

root = true

[*]
charset = utf-8
insert_final_newline = true
trim_trailing_whitespace = true
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4

[*.{json,yml,yaml,md}]
indent_size = 2

[*.{ts,html,scss,css}]
indent_size = 2

[*.{csproj,props,targets,slnx,xml}]
indent_size = 2

[*.cs]
# Namespaces and usings
csharp_style_namespace_declarations = file_scoped:suggestion
dotnet_sort_system_directives_first = true
dotnet_separate_import_directive_groups = false
dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0005.severity = suggestion

# var preferences: use var when the type is apparent
csharp_style_var_for_built_in_types = false:suggestion
csharp_style_var_when_type_is_apparent = true:suggestion
csharp_style_var_elsewhere = false:suggestion

# Modern syntax is offered silently; working code is not modernized mechanically
csharp_style_prefer_primary_constructors = true:silent
dotnet_style_prefer_collection_expression = when_types_loosely_match:silent
csharp_style_prefer_switch_expression = true:silent
csharp_style_prefer_pattern_matching = true:silent

# Braces and expression bodies
csharp_prefer_braces = true:suggestion
csharp_style_expression_bodied_methods = false:silent
csharp_style_expression_bodied_properties = true:silent

# Naming: PascalCase for types and members, camelCase for parameters and locals
dotnet_naming_symbols.types_and_members.applicable_kinds = class, struct, interface, enum, method, property, event, delegate
dotnet_naming_style.pascal_case.capitalization = pascal_case
dotnet_naming_rule.types_and_members_pascal.symbols = types_and_members
dotnet_naming_rule.types_and_members_pascal.style = pascal_case
dotnet_naming_rule.types_and_members_pascal.severity = suggestion

dotnet_naming_symbols.interfaces.applicable_kinds = interface
dotnet_naming_style.i_prefix.required_prefix = I
dotnet_naming_style.i_prefix.capitalization = pascal_case
dotnet_naming_rule.interfaces_i_prefix.symbols = interfaces
dotnet_naming_rule.interfaces_i_prefix.style = i_prefix
dotnet_naming_rule.interfaces_i_prefix.severity = suggestion

dotnet_naming_symbols.parameters_and_locals.applicable_kinds = parameter, local
dotnet_naming_style.camel_case.capitalization = camel_case
dotnet_naming_rule.parameters_and_locals_camel.symbols = parameters_and_locals
dotnet_naming_rule.parameters_and_locals_camel.style = camel_case
dotnet_naming_rule.parameters_and_locals_camel.severity = suggestion

Health checks may be called frequently: avoid expensive queries, long external
timeouts, large allocations, full business workflows, and Error-level logs for

Log information that helps diagnose or operate the system, and choose log
levels by operational meaning, not by how unusual an event feels.

Avoid:

- **Trace / Debug** — detailed diagnostics for troubleshooting (sensitive-data
  rules apply at every level: `security.md`).
- **Information** — normal meaningful events: a background job completed, an
  important business operation completed, a runtime lifecycle event. Avoid
  logging every internal method call.
- **Warning** — an unexpected or degraded condition the application recovered
  from: fallback used, retry sequence exhausted but another path succeeded,
  optional dependency unavailable, unusual but handled state.
- **Error** — an operation failed and needs investigation (which outcomes are
  not errors: `error-handling.md` § Exception Logging).
- **Critical** — the application or a major subsystem cannot continue safely.

Use `ILogger.BeginScope` when several entries share contextual data:

Prefer platform/runtime trace identifiers when they already provide adequate
request correlation. Add an explicit correlation identifier only when an
integration or operational requirement needs one; validate or normalize an
identifier accepted from an external client before propagating it. Propagate
correlation/tracing context across outbound calls with the project's chosen
tracing or HTTP infrastructure.

For external calls check cancellation propagation, timeout strategy,
idempotency where relevant, retry safety, failure translation, and
disposal/lifetime behavior (`performance.md` § Outbound Calls). Do not demand
retries for operations that are not safe to retry.

`GET` is safe and idempotent, `PUT` is idempotent, `DELETE` is idempotent in
intended state semantics, `POST` is generally not idempotent. When a repeated
`POST` must not create duplicate effects, consider an `Idempotency-Key` header
whose key the server associates with the request and result; reusing a key with
a materially different payload is reasonably a `409`. Do not claim idempotency
merely because duplicate requests are unlikely.

Named, typed, and keyed clients are all valid; choose the simplest model for
the consumer and its lifetime. Outbound API clients belong in Infrastructure.
Retry and circuit-breaker behavior is added only when its semantics fit.

Configure retries, circuit breakers, hedging, fallback, or pipelines with
`references/resilience.md`. Before enabling retry, determine whether the
failure is transient, whether the operation is safe to repeat, whether the
remote API supports idempotency, and whether a retry may duplicate side effects.
For POST/PATCH and other state-changing operations, retry safety comes from
API-defined idempotency keys, naturally idempotent semantics, or explicit
deduplication; do not assume every PUT or DELETE implementation is
operationally safe merely because the method is defined as idempotent.

Check-by-reference against `performance.md` § Outbound Calls and
`architecture.md` § Layer Placement: a new `HttpClient` per request; typed,
keyed, or named clients made mandatory universally; retries on unsafe
operations without idempotency analysis; infinite or poorly bounded retries;
`HttpResponseMessage` leaking across boundaries; ignored cancellation; dynamic
tokens in shared `DefaultRequestHeaders`; every upstream failure mapped to the
same status; resilience pipelines added without understanding their behavior.

Resilience policies match failure and operation semantics. Circuit breakers
help when repeated dependency failures would otherwise consume resources or
amplify an outage. Do not add resilience mechanisms merely because they are
available, and observe retries, timeouts, and circuit behavior when they
materially affect operations.

The standard handler is useful when its behavior fits the remote API; it is not
mandatory for every client. Review its retry behavior carefully for
state-changing requests. Client lifetime and configuration: `httpclient-factory`.

Plausibly transient failures: selected network failures, temporary service
unavailability, rate limiting when retry is allowed, transient provider-specific
database failures. Not retried: validation errors, authentication/authorization
failures, permanent `404` outcomes, deterministic business rejection, and
non-idempotent operations without a duplicate-prevention strategy.

If the answer is "duplicate side effect", automatic retry is unsafe. Use an
API-supported idempotency mechanism when appropriate; do not invent a
client-side `Idempotency-Key` unless the remote service supports that contract.

## Hedging

Hedging issues parallel or delayed duplicate attempts. Use it only for
operations that are safe to execute multiple times, typically idempotent reads
against interchangeable endpoints; do not hedge state-changing operations.

## Database Resilience

Do not wrap normal persistence operations in a generic application-level retry
pipeline. When the persistence provider supports transient retry through its
execution strategy or provider configuration, prefer that mechanism, and handle
transaction/retry interaction according to the provider's guidance (persistence
knowledge skill). An HTTP retry policy is not automatically appropriate for
database operations.

Retrying message publication requires understanding the broker and delivery
semantics; a retry may produce duplicate delivery. Use idempotent consumers,
broker-supported deduplication, outbox patterns, or similar mechanisms when the
business requirement needs them, and do not claim exactly-once delivery because
a retry policy exists.

Check-by-reference against `performance.md` § Outbound Calls: retrying every
exception or HTTP status; retrying unsafe writes without idempotency analysis;
retrying client cancellation; circuit breakers without a failure scenario;
fallback values that conceal incorrect business results; hedged writes; generic
retry wrappers around persistence without understanding provider behavior;
stacked handlers with overlapping strategies; unbounded retry/timeout
combinations.

retry can duplicate effects (`performance.md` § Outbound Calls). Caller
